summary: NISAR Canopy is an open-source console for the NASA-ISRO NISAR radar mission. It closes the gap between raw synthetic aperture radar products and the people who need answers from them. Draw a box on a map and the app queries the ASF archive for every NISAR scene crossing it, with browse imagery and acquisition dates. Pick a scene and run the analysis that matters: GCOV clipping, RVI, change detection, time series and GeoTIFF export; SME2 soil moisture at 200 m (DSG, PMI, TSR); or GUNW coherence and wrapped/unwrapped phase from a 12-day pair. Every run lands in a job panel with history, log, images, JSON and GeoTIFFs, and the log stores the exact command plan, so a result is reproducible instead of being a screenshot. Built with FastAPI, React and Leaflet over a Python radar pipeline.
details:
What it does. NISAR Canopy takes a user from a place on the map to a finished radar analysis in one console. The user draws a bounding box on a Leaflet map; the backend queries the ASF DAAC search API and returns every NISAR scene that intersects it, with browse imagery and acquisition dates. Any box works: the console is not tied to a study area, a country or a campaign, and the same flow applies wherever the mission acquires data over land or water.

How it works. Selecting a scene exposes the NISAR product families. GCOV covers amplitude work: clipping, radar vegetation index, change detection, time series, GeoTIFF export, water masks, active-fire overlay and optical fusion with Sentinel-2. SME2 provides soil moisture from the soil moisture product, with the DSG, PMI and TSR retrievals available side by side so they can be compared instead of trusted individually. GUNW provides interferometry: coherence, and wrapped and unwrapped phase for the repeat-pass pair. Each analysis becomes a queued job, and a panel shows its history, live log, rendered images, JSON metadata and GeoTIFF outputs. The interface is the same for every product, so learning the console once is enough.

Benefits. The radiometric and geometric work stays inside a versioned Python pipeline, so the interface shows only a map and a job list. Every job records the exact command plan it ran, which makes a result reproducible and auditable rather than a screenshot. Outputs are plain GeoTIFFs that open in any GIS viewer, so a user does not need a specialised SAR workstation to check the science. The search happens on browse imagery, so the pair is chosen before downloading heavy products instead of after.

Intended impact. The mission produces an enormous volume of radar data, and most of it stays hard to reach for people who are not radar specialists. NISAR Canopy is aimed at response teams, environmental monitoring groups, land-use analysts and students: choose a place, choose an analysis, and get a reproducible artifact with the recipe attached. Reproducibility is the design goal, because a change map nobody can re-run has limited operational value. Because the workflow is place-agnostic, the same console serves a deforestation question, a flood, a fire scar, a soil-moisture series or an interferometric pair without changing tools.

Tools. Python for the radar pipeline (NumPy, rasterio and GDAL, h5py, PyProj, tifffile, Matplotlib, pystac-client, planetary-computer); FastAPI and uvicorn for the API and the job queue; React with Leaflet, TypeScript and Vite for the front end; Docker for packaging; uv for reproducible dependency locking. The project ships a network-free unit test suite covering the API contract, box validation, the browse proxy, on-disk scene detection, the timeline and the exact command plan of each product.

Creativity and factors considered. One reprojection-and-cut path is shared by very different NISAR products, so a change analysis, a soil-moisture map and an interferogram all come out of the same geometry pipeline: the user changes the question, not the tool. The design also treats the command plan as a first-class output rather than a debugging detail. Practical constraints shaped the choices: a single scene is large, so data lives on a local disk outside the repository; the app runs and executes subprocesses without authentication, so it listens on loopback only; and the console declares what it cannot do instead of hiding it.

What it does not prove. The NISAR collections used are provisional, radar measures structure rather than biomass, backscatter also responds to soil moisture, rain and acquisition geometry, and the reported area depends on the pixel scale. Short repeat-pass pairs, a paired control area and the difference between polarizations keep those effects visible, but none of them turns the console into an operational inventory. It is an exploration and auditing tool, not a certified monitoring service.
